utterances.text: No, nothing would happen then because at that time, I think not everything worked -- not everything was in perfect order so there were no instruments of coercion, that is to use -- to sanction the men, simply somebody else would be called up and he would be sent off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were there any attempts to bring in such a man because he was needed?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Could you clarify the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that a determined effort was made to bring a particular man in if he had failed to respond, because his knowledge or his expertise was needed. So did you ever ask the police to bring him in?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Could you please tell me at what time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before that, during the Tomasevic or during the Staff, if somebody wanted to dodge such summons, then he could do that, isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, when the Vitez Brigade was formed, then it became less easy to dodge this duty but it was still possible?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, at that time, did you know, were you aware basically every conscripts that responded to summons did it of his own will?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me ask you, Witness Ceko, the first time that you joined the work of the Staff and that was, here you told us, was in April/May, 1992, the Municipal HVO Staff in Vitez, I mean, did anyone tell you, "Mr. Ceko, excuse me, but you're going to do this. So you start here and you are bound to attend."

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No, never. I volunteered and that is how I started working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you volunteered why?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, I volunteered because I realised that I had to do something to contribute to the defence of my place of my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does this apply to Mario Cerkez too?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Those soldiers of yours, now that we've already formed the brigade, would you agree that this list of the active duty totalled some 300 men at the time we are referring to after the brigade was formed?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, I agree it was around 300 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when people from the list were summoned to go to front lines against the Serb army, how long did one shift last?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: The shifts were between seven and ten days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, the brigade held with those men from the battalion, from the battalion's list, the sector at Slatka Vode/Kamenjas, that part, is it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, and I mean before 16th of April, did the Vitez Brigade have any other task, any other area of responsibility as you soldiers put it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Before 16th of April, yes. At that time, between November or December 1992, that was its own area, that is, Jajce. After the fall of Jajce in November, December, we began to send our shifts to Slatka Vode, up there to the -- near Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was still during the Staff's time?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, it was during the Staff's time, and it went on until April. And in Tomasevic's time, yes, in Tomasevic's time, in Staff's time and in Viteska Brigade's time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And when those soldiers would come back from their mission -- so they had spent seven days in Jajce, or, if we are referring to this time near to 16th of April, seven days on Kamenjas at the front lines up there -- what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, having completed a shift, seven days or ten days -- it varied -- they would come back home and they would naturally return home, return to their families or to their jobs, because when they would complete their shifts, they would become civilians again and they would go about their daily business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if the brigade would need the same soldier two days later, what would happen then?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, he would be summoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he would be reactivated?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, he would be reactivated. He would be free until he would be summoned again and before he left to the shift again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But always from that list?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. The list was always the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. His Honour, Judge Bennouna, already asked some questions about the evening of the 15th of April, so there is no need to go back to that. I'm just trying to see if we've covered all the points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, yes, I received some details for the Chamber regarding the day of the 15th of April, but now I'd like to put questions to the witness regarding the morning of the 16th. He said that he left at 5.00 in the morning and that Mr. Cerkez arrived at 6.00 in the morning on the 16th. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, that was so. I went -- I left home at 5.00 to go to the command, and I saw Cerkez there later. I think it was around 6.00. I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But my first question is as follows: Why did you go to the command at 5.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: At 5.00 in the morning on the 16th of April, 1993, I went to the command, because the night before, at the short briefing that we had, if you remember, there was a possibility of an ABiH attack along the Kruscica-Vranjska direction, in the direction of the centre of the town of Vitez. So the degree of alertness or preparedness was raised, and that was why I left early, at 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you say that Mr. Cerkez came -- arrived at 6.00 that morning?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts. Around 6.00, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us whether there was a meeting on that morning when you got there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: That morning -- because not far from that I had the depot, not far from the headquarters of the brigade, that is, next to the municipal hall, so I went there too. And if there was a meeting that morning, I was not present at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what did you do that morning?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: That morning I spent most of the time, that morning and the day, in the materiel depot, because I had a small office there. And I was simply checking the state, what we had at our disposal; if there was a serious conflict, what we had available there, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there any fighting that morning, as was anticipated? Was there an attack towards Kruscica, as you mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: That morning, sometime around half past 5.00, several shells hit the centre of the town of Vitez itself, that is, near the headquarters of -- near the cinema, and one could hear gunfire from all sides. And there was a general melee there, and it was in the morning, around half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had received instructions the day -- the night before. Did they all relate only to instructions regarding the defence of the Vitez town?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. Only along the Kruscica-Vranjska directions, and that is where we expected the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you received no instructions as to starting any offensive?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to the shells that fell in Vitez on that morning of the 16th of April, you don't know where they came from, do you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. From surrounding hills, I guess. From surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which action did you take on that 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: I, you mean? Well, I was in this materiel depot. And since this gunfire started in the morning, and there was a general confusion, a general melee, I had to be present in the depot all the time, because some people, as they were moving, people were coming and asking for weapons and other things so as to defend themselves, so that I had to be in the depot all the time, practically, because I was in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you provide a lot of equipment that day?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No. No. I did not issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just told us that there were a lot of people coming to see you on that morning on the 16th of April in order to obtain weapons or ammunition, and you didn't give any?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, people came, but I did not say many people came. Men came to ask for it, but I didn't have any weapons or equipment or uniforms, so that at the time I didn't issue them with it. So I had nothing to supply them with, and so I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen. Something has got to be explained to this Court, because I fail to understand your version of events. You said that the night before you met, that Mr. Cerkez was called as a matter of urgency, that the wedding was cancelled, there was an imminent threat of attack, that you got up very early in the morning, and then nothing happens in the morning -- during the day of the 16th of April. Could you explain all this to us, because we don't understand very well what you're telling us. You're telling us that there's a lot of chaos on the 16th of April, that it was a situation of alert that had been triggered, that the wedding had been cancelled, so that you were expecting the worst on the 16th. And then you say -- you end up saying that nothing happened on that day. So I'd like to know what happened, what did happen on that day. What was happening that justified this commotion on the 16th of April? There's something missing in the events you are relating.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in the evening of the 15th, after the short brief, I left my men on duty in the depot, my men who were there, just in case something happened. And then in the morning I went to the depot, that is, to the headquarters of the brigade. And around half past 5.00, several shells hit the centre of the town of Vitez, near the headquarters, that is, near the cinema. And gunfire came from all sides. Later on I learned that there had been an attack up there at Poculica, followed by Kruscica and Vranjska and Krdo Dol [phoen] and Krcevine, surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the 16th of April, not about the 15th; is that so?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: All I said, that on the 15th I assigned men to stand guard at the depot and then I went back home. And now I'm talking about the 16th, when the town was shelled, when we heard the gunfire from all sides. And I was notified that there had been an attack at Poculica, that all the Croat villagers in that village had been captured, and that was followed by an attack from the direction of Kruscica and Vranjska and surrounding villages, I think at Krcevine and Jardol, along that route. And when I said that I was not issuing anyone with anything, then this is what I meant: I didn't issue, with any weapons, those men who were not members of the brigade. That is, at that time, the brigade had only one battalion, and when the fire began, when the attack began, then some men who were not members of the brigade came to the depot trying to get something. But at that time, the situation in the depot was critical. It was not satisfactory. We simply had no weapons at all. We had some ammunition and we didn't have any materiel, that is, uniforms, clothing, and the rest. And I said those men who came of their own, I did not issue them with anything. But that morning [as interpreted] also the general mobilisation was proclaimed, because the men were gathered and were sent to the front lines where there were major conflicts, and I had nothing to give them. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who went to see you who were not members of the brigade, were they organised or did they come on an individual basis?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: They were individuals who came, of their own initiative. And there were also those who were summoned later on, those who responded to summons. Because we've already heard about the conflict. It was escalating and general mobilisation was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I should continue from the point where the Honourable Judge stopped. When was mobilisation declared?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, I said I can't remember. I know it was declared immediately that day, but whether it was immediately in the morning, I don't know. It was probably sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have noticed a rather serious mistake here in the transcript, page 52, line 6. It says that mobilisation was in the morning, and the witness said "on that day." And now he said that he thought that it was not in the morning of that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are sure the mobilisation was declared on that day, but you do not know when?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was mobilisation declared the previous day?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No. No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to the Honourable Judge's questions, you mentioned various places: Jardol, Poculica, Kruscica. What happened in those places? Tell us what happened in those places. Who attacked whom?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: The BH army attacked the men who were village guards at that time. They were guarding their villages and they attacked them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That morning or that night, or perhaps even before that, what do you know? I mean, what happened at Kuber?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: The previous night, the 15th of April, in the evening, that is, the duty officer at the brigade command received information that there were some problems at Kuber, that the BH army attacked Kuber. However, the duty officer did not manage to establish contact at all and he did not know whether this was correct or not, until the next morning. And the next morning it was learned that indeed, on the evening of the 15th Kuber had been attacked and that Kuber had been lost and that some men had been killed. There are two men that are missing until the present day, that are still registered as missing. So I forgot to mention Kuber a few minutes ago. I forgot that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me please, Mr. Ceko: As an inhabitant of that area -- and roughly speaking, you were familiar with the situation: where, whose military was, et cetera -- for you personally, for you personally, without anyone having explained it to you, what does this information mean for you at that point in time, that something was going on in Kuber? What is the first thing that that came to your mind?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, the first thing that came to my mind was that the BH army attacked the Viteska Brigade that was at Kuber, because they were right next to each other at Kuber. This is a dominant feature. This is where they both were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we could explain this to the Court. This was never explained before, I think. As soon as resistance against the Serbs started in the early months of 1992 --

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- there were some guards at Kuber, right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those were mixed guards, right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, they were not mixed guards. This -- Kuber is actually a broader notion, but this is a dominant feature between Vitez and Zenica. That is where one of our groups was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] -- and then there was also a Muslim group that was next to them, so they were next to each other, but they were not together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a request from the interpreters for the witness to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So early in 1992, both sides, at that time, had their guards up there at Kuber with what intention in mind?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. They stood guard up there in Kuber with the intention of observing the JNA movements in Zenica. At that time, the JNA was in Zenica in barracks, and from up there you could see barracks and movements, and that is why this group was located up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were observing the JNA who was your only enemy at that time?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this observation in more active or more passive form continued all the way up to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us complete the subject of Kuber once we've embarked on it. The next few days, the BH army took all the dominant features in Kuber; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO had to withdraw from Kuber?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from that moment onwards, throughout the conflict, the BH army had Kuber under its control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. But the HVO, I mean the brigade withdrew a bit lower and that is where it established its defence line. The BH army was up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to hear from you, that you were below. Could we again use the map we used yesterday and have it put before the witness. Number 85, I didn't really plan to go into all of this, but -- Mr. Ceko, please take a look at the map. You're a local man. Please show Kuber, the entire chain of mountains that is called Kuber. A bit to the right, please, Mr. Usher, please, a bit to the right. [In English] Sorry, on the opposite size. Yeah, that's it.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Kuber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could I ask that the picture is from the higher aspect -- yeah, okay, perfect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show Vitez now?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: There.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Zenica?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up there where it says the 7th Muslim, up there, over the name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean for you that Kuber is a natural wall, a wall, so to speak, between Zenica and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that when the army took Kuber -- could you show me on which side of Kuber was the part that was held by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why are we going into all this detail? Could you explain what you intend by it? We've got the point about Kuber. It's a large feature, although quite why the Viteska Brigade is guarding it, we don't know. Now, do we need any more detail about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just got where I wanted to come, to show that there was actually an attack the next morning, at least on this detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There was a report of an attack, that's the evidence you have, on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then witness said on my direct question that the next couple of days, the army took over Kuber gradually. It started, obviously, on 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why was the Viteska Brigade responsible for Kuber?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: The Viteska Brigade, I don't know. I didn't understand your question. I mean, what do you mean "responsible"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought your evidence was that the Viteska Brigade had guards up on Kuber. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No. Viteska Brigade did not guard Kuber. It was men who were guarding it up there. It was those village guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: From where did they come?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: From their own villages, Kratine, Nadioci, below Kuber. The locals from underneath Kuber, the villages of Nadioci and Kratine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ceko, to complete the question put by the Presiding Judge, could you tell us whether there is any correlation or relationship between the Viteska Brigade and the village guards, because you say that when the attacks that you anticipated took place, the village guards were guarding those places. So what was the relationship between the Viteska Brigade and those guards, village guards?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: At that time, the relationship between Viteska Brigade and the village guards was nonexistent. There wasn't any. Because sometimes, men from one of the battalions of the Viteska Brigade would be on the village guards. Of course, when they finished their shift against the ARS, they would be free and, from time to time, they would be sent to the village guards because they were self-organised, they made their own shifts and that was in various villages and that was Kuber, too, because Kuber is considered to be a village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Ceko. Do you mean to say that the Viteska Brigade had no authority whatsoever over the village guards?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, it did not until the 16th. It did not have authority over village guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did it start having authority over the village guards?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: When general mobilisation was declared on the 16th sometime in the afternoon, and then call-up papers were sent out. Men who were on the village guards and who were not actively engaged anywhere in this way became members of the Viteska Brigade. So, that is to say, that from the 16th onwards, all became members of the Viteska Brigade. Until then, there was only one battalion numbering about 300 men in the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps just another detail in this connection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said from then onwards, the village guards joined the brigade, but that was a process, wasn't it? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say now that from a given point onwards, all village guards became members of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: From the moment, from the moment they were mobilised, they became members of the Viteska Brigade. They are resubordinated to the command to the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mobilisation was declared?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it is established who has done what and who is doing what and lists were established et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, how long did this process last, one day, two days, three days? What are we talking about, at least for the main part, what about -- I'm sorry, perhaps I am complicating things a bit too much. No, let's go back to this later. Another thing that was mentioned here. When you explained this situation in relation to Kuber, Mr. Ceko, you were not the operations officer of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No, I was not. I came from civilian life. Even when I did my military service in the former JNA, I did not have any rank. I was never interested in the military. I was a normal man, a civilian, and that is how I started gaining experience from 1992 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you've mentioned these places already, on the first day, on the second day, during these critical days, did you find out what happened in Sivrino Selo? Were there any events that occurred there or not?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. Sivrino Selo is a mixed community. A few families -- well, Miskovici what's it called -- oh, I can't say now -- but they were all detained in Sivrino Selo. Yes, yes, it's called the hamlet of Miskovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What detained them?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: It was the BH army who detained them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Croats from the Croat part of the village were detained?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps yet another detail. Let's go back to the 15th of April in the evening, the meeting that you attended at the brigade. After the meeting, I mean did Cerkez leave before you or after you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: You mean on the 15th in the evening?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: He left after me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and your fellow officers who stayed there after Cerkez, did you discuss all of this amongst yourselves -- did you talk about whether this information that Cerkez had received was plausible or not?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, yes. When Cerkez left, we officers from the brigade discussed this, and I got the impression from this discussion that most of my colleagues from the command believe that there would not be a serious conflict, that perhaps there could be a minor incident and that everything would end at that. That was my estimate on the basis of the discussion I had with my colleagues because before that, there were also such pieces of information that were received but in the morning ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that on several occasions before, there were such alarms and that the state of readiness was brought up?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during these earlier warnings that something would happen, did something actually happen or did nothing happen?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, nothing happened. And that is why we believed that nothing would happen, perhaps that there would be a minor incident but nothing of a more serious nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness Ceko, tell me, please, your primary concern on the 16th of April was to get ready in order to carry out the duty that you were supposed to carry out. What did you do? You said a few minutes ago that your supplies were very scarce. You said that had you no weapons at all and that you had very little ammunition and you didn't have other equipment.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, on the evening of the 15th, I looked through documentation and I saw that the situation was one that, indeed, does cause concern. And the next day, I contacted the Assistant Commander for Logistics of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, both orally and in writing and I asked him for materiel. I especially thought that if there would be mobilisation that it would not be possible to equip everyone and to provide them with the necessary equipment. So I contacted Central Bosnia considerably because I asked them for more supplies of materiel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As assistant commander in the brigade command, is it natural for you to establish communication with the assistant commander in the higher command?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as your area of responsibility is strictly concerned, that is to say logistics, you don't have to go through your own commander and ask for this from the superior command?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: I don't have to go through my own commander, but it is natural that I provide information to the commander so that he can help me with the organisation of such affairs but, of course, I can also go through my superior commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia? Who was the person who was the Assistant Commander for Logistics?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: The Assistant Commander for Logistics of the Operative Zone was Franjo Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a good cooperation with him?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there follow up on those requests? What was the situation with supplies during the following days?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of my request, and I suppose that Commander Mario Cerkez, as I had notified him that we are very short of supplies and that we were very -- our ammunition supply was meagre and everything, he must have had contact with the commander. So on the evening of the 16th we were sent a small supply of ammunition and several times, once again in the days that followed, but those were all very small quantities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the situation with weapons, because the mobilisation was already underway, whence the weapons for mobilised men?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Mobilised men. Quite a number of people had weapons. That is, village guards, they had weapons with them, and also, perhaps, some other men who were mobilised or perhaps had weapons in some other unit or simply -- one didn't know before that he had any weapons because he was not recorded, but he might have had some weapons at home. They had weapons, but other men simply didn't, and we couldn't arm them because we did not have in store any weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means that those men who were mobilised from amongst the village guards, that they were desirable conscripts candidates for mobilisation because they had their weapons?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereas they didn't have to hold true of those others because they may not have had their weapons?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let me ask you, Witness Ceko, in your -- those weapons came to your depot and left. Before and after, what sources, what was the provenience of those weapons that arrived in Bosnia, as a man who was there and handled those weapons?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, yes, in the early days, there was this illegal arming. That is, people themselves, people from some villages sold their property, people even sold their cows in order to purchase rifles. So some people -- that is how some of the people were armed. And most other people set out to take the JNA barracks in Slimena, and that is how people collected from there most of the weapons and the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the Municipal Staff or later on during the time of brigades, did the HVO government manage to procure a significant quantity of weapons in an organised manner?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No, not in a more organised manner. A more organised supply of weapons did not begin before mid-1992 when the -- when the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia was set up. I think it was sometime in mid-1992, I'm not sure about the date, and it was only then that the supply of weapons was better organised, but where the weapons came from I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means that the Operative Zone had its own line of supply and you, the brigade subsequently -- when the brigades were formed, had your own line of supplies?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Both of you are going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You expected -- will you please explain it in your own words?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: The brigade did not undertake the organisation of the supply of weapons by itself, but when the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia was set up, it -- the weapons and ammunition and all the other military gear was done more systematically, and that began sometime in the summer of 1992, when this zone was set up. And from then on, all the logistical support of the brigades went to the Superior Commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, to the logistics department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us go back to the conflict. The conflict broke out, and you needed supplies. The Vitez pocket in those first two or three days was increasingly surrounded which was the only land route that you could use for your supplies.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, practically as of the 16th of April 1993, Central Bosnia, the Lasva Valley, was isolated, so there were no land routes left. And since from the depot of the Operative Zone, because they were down to the critical left of ammunition, they organised their convoy that went through Busovaca to Sebesic because that was, at that time, the only land route that could be used for our supplies. That is through Busovaca and Sebesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show it on the map? The map is next to you.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm not an operations man and I am not sure I can find my way about maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps this is not important. I thought perhaps you could help us. But at any rate, going through these points that you mention which were used by your convoys --

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us: When was it that the BH army cut off this route for the convoys, once and for all, when it could not used anymore?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: That route was cut off once and for all in late June 1993. I think, to be more exact, that it was on the 15th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as of that day, there is no land route available to you for your supplies? Land route, I mean --

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No. As of that day -- well, there were some brave individuals who would use a mountain pass to get through Sebesic, and they brought what they could carry, perhaps, but that was the only way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us: As regards that route around Sebesic, we're referring to convoys which used mules and horses?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because this is a mountain path, very narrow. The only way to -- one could use only mules or horses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No vehicles?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no, no. We used horses, and that was the only way of transport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the front lines were defined in the municipal area, what was your other task, apart from weapons, that is, ammunition? What were you expected to supply your troops with now?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: When the front lines were defined in the municipality of Vitez, one of my tasks, one of my hardest tasks, perhaps, was to organise the support with food supplies; that is, I had to organise kitchens, personnel, in all the villages. And I wasted -- I spent a lot of time organising it, to feed the troops. And it was established -- it took place only some 10 or 15 days after the conflict broke out. And until that time, these troops were fed by local -- by villagers. And the troops too, more or less; every soldier went back to his village. And there were problems when we tried to get a man from one village to send to some other. Where there was more stronger attack, it was a major problem, because everybody went to the boundaries of his own village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that people saw this war as a defence of their own hearth, of their own village?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during your work for the HVO -- you were an officer, you had a function there -- did you ever hear that there was some official or unofficial policy of persecution and disturbance of the Muslim population, the civilians, by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: As an HVO officer, I affirm that there never existed, official or unofficial, policy of persecution or harassment of Muslims in the territory of the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Officer Ceko: In those days after the formation of the brigade, the Vitez Brigade, who was responsible? What unit provided security, took care of the security of the building and personnel of the command of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: As of the formation of the brigade, the security of the building -- and personnel, of course, in the command -- was in charge of a small platoon of the military police, the 4th Battalion of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this platoon under the command of the Brigade Commander?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No. They were under the command of the Commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in point of fact, within this general term, "security," what was the role of that platoon? What did it do?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, its principal task was to guard the building, the whole building, the reception desk; then the civilians and everybody else who might come to the headquarters, to the command of the brigade, so to ask of them from the reception desk to the command officers. Those were the tasks of the particular platoon which was securing the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you called that unit the brigade military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, yes. Most -- most people -- most people are members of the command even, and that same building -- in that same building there were other people too. There were the radio and television station, and most of them referred to it as the "brigade military police," because they were with us every day, from the very beginning. They were with us in the mess and so on and so forth. They lived and worked with us, sharing the premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know, when did this, in inverted commas, "brigade military police," was truly placed under the command of the brigade command, that is, became part of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, I do know when that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was it, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: That was in August, perhaps mid-August 1993. The order was issued that it was to be subordinated to the commander of the brigade, because when there was a minor task to do, then it was difficult to do it. Usually in case of -- in such cases when some of the conscripts failed to report, and then a request had to be sent to the 4th Battalion of the Military Police to bring in the men, and then they would have to issue the order to the policemen to bring those men. So it was difficult, really, to do it, and that was why it was decided to attach them to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that even those routine jobs, such as the one that you mentioned, to bring in a military conscripts who failed to report, that actually it was up to the goodwill of those policemen of yours whether they would do it, or you had to ask their command to do that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... to send a request to their command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ceko, as of the 16th of April onward, for a while, in the building of the command, in the building of the cinema, or rather the Workers' University, as it was called, there were also interned some people. Did you see those people interned there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those were citizens of Muslim ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you know if those people were also interned in some other places, or rather, at some other locations in the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. I do know. In the building of the former social auditing service and the chess club in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see those other locations where they were interned, in the auditing office and the chess club?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which HVO unit controlled those locations? Which unit guarded them at those locations?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: The internees in those places were guarded by the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you know if there were some interned persons at other locations outside the town?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. They were also in the Dubravica elementary school and the veterinary station at Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who controlled those two locations?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Those two locations were controlled by the special purpose unit Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the elementary school in Dubravica, that is where Vitezovi had their base; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at Rijeka, the veterinary station, they also used to gather there all the time?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, yes, they gathered there very often, because the commander of that unit lived at Rijeka, in the forester's lodge, quite close to the veterinary station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "commander," who was that commander?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: It was Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that he is deceased?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the way, you knew Darko Kraljevic, because it's not all that far away from your house?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him, because it's a rather small place, so we all knew one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that physically he was very much like Mario Cerkez, about the same height?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. They were about the same height. They're both dark-haired. Yes, they looked very much alike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But there's another difference. In Dubravica -- no. Let me try to phrase it clearer. In the early days, it was the auditing office, the chess club, the cinema. Could you tell the Court if only men were detained there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. Only men, and only men of military age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you quite sure that at that time there were no women there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: I passed by very often and I never saw them, nor did I hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we have the evidence. I may have missed it. Who guarded the cinema?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The witness just said the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, he's going too fast. It's difficult to follow. Remember that we have to follow this. I certainly heard the chess club and I certainly heard the auditing office, but I didn't hear the cinema. Is that right, Mr. Ceko? Who guarded the detainees in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: The detainees in the cinema were guarded by the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And who commanded the military police in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: I recall that one of the commanders was Anto Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ceko, I suppose -- or rather, do you know who was this Kovac's superior?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Anto Kovac's -- the commander of this platoon securing the command of the brigade, his commander was Pasko Ljubicic, the Commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would know precisely who was between him, that is, the Commander of the 4th Battalion, and this down there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No, I don't. I think that for a while it was Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do not have any precise information, or is it the time frame that bothers you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No. It is the time frame that confuses me. And of course men changed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But the seat of the 4th Battalion of the military police was in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many metres is that away? A hundred metres away from you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Less than 100 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just two minor points in relation to the interned persons. You know, and you saw, that at these places of internment in the cinema in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Kovacic please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in the SDK [as interpreted], in the chess club, and in the cinema, it was only men who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get Mr. Kovacic's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, the interpreters didn't get your question. They are also asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ceko, we will have to go back. I have to put this question again to you. In the school in Dubravica, who was there? Who were the persons who were interned there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: In the school in Dubravica, persons of Muslim ethnicity were interned there. There were some able-bodied men, there were women, there were children. That's what I heard. I was never there, but that's what I heard. I heard that it was that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the location of your office and in view of the fact that from time to time you would come to the cinema building where your headquarters was, on those occasions did you ever see any person being mistreated? Did you ever see anything like that yourself?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No, I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of any mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No, I did not hear of any mistreatment either, any mistreatment of the interned persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, see doctors coming to visit, Red Cross and things like that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, I did see a group of doctors with the Red Cross. They came into the cinema. They came into the cinema hall and they talked to these people and they helped them and they asked them things. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity of seeing interned persons being visited by their families?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that quite often. They had visitors all the time. As a matter of fact, on one occasion I was present when a man's daughter came, and he was allowed to go home and take a bath, and then he returned to the cinema.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity of seeing these persons taken out, taken out to work for the military or for the defence, to dig trenches, for example?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No, I did not have the opportunity of seeing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you hear about that later, that there were such cases?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. Later I did hear about a couple of such cases. I personally did not see this, but I know that at that time work units had already been established for digging trenches at the defence lines, and of course there were Muslims and Croats and Serbs, naturally, in those work units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of establishing work units and taking care of them?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: It was the defence department, the civil defence unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the defence department? That was part of the municipal government in Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ceko, since there has been lots of diverse information in this trial, we'll ask you to help us out with something else. When the conflict already broke out in 1993, are you sure that the headquarters of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia is in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, in the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the hotel, that is also where the 4th Battalion of the Military Police has its headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military police, the members of the military police, they had permanent accommodation where?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: I think they were in the hotel in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were some of them in another building quite close to your depot later?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the building where the Court is nowadays, where the Court is now; that is to say, the building right next to the depot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw a certain number of soldiers from the military police staying there 24 hours, around the clock, not going home?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: They were there all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to those we've mentioned just now, in town there were also the so-called PPN Vitezovi. They operated in the area too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. The Vitezovi were also in the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From time to time, or permanently, did the PPN Zuti come to the area and operate there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: The PPN Zuti did -- the PPN Tvrtkovci came to Vitez from time to time, and then there were also the PZO, and then also the members of the Travnicka Brigade, then Jure Francetic, the Zenica battalion, and also others. Also some from the Ludvig Pavlovic unit were in Vitez from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ludvig Pavlovic, as an organised unit, it is mentioned that they left already in February 1993.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know that Bruno Busic's unit left sometime in January 1993. They were in Travnik, where we were, where we had the command of Stjepan Tomasevic, and I am not sure that all of them had left later, I mean all the Ludvig Pavlovic people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps let us explain in a word or two. The PPN Zuti, whose unit was that? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: That was the unit from Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, to the best of your knowledge, all these mentioned units, who are they subordinated to? Who is their superior, their joint superior?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who commanded them and who their superior command was. I just know that there were problems and I know that they were not under Blaskic's command. But who commanded them exactly, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that at some moments Blaskic could order them and sometimes he could not?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, they could not have been ordered by anybody, more or less. Those were units that perhaps you could agree on something with them on a sort of human basis, but you could not order them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think, Mr. Ceko, that your commander, Mario Cerkez, could have commanded any one of these units?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: All those units had some kind of insignia which made it more or less clear that they belonged to the Croat side in this conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were different insignia; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. There were different insignia. There were some recognisable insignia. There were some different uniforms. There were some black uniforms. However, the majority, the majority, had HVO insignia and camouflage uniforms. Some PPN units, special purpose units, in addition to the HVO patch, had the patch of their brigade, the emblem of their -- and also pistols, holsters, et cetera; however, most of them had HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that not at all points in time and not at every place was it clear, when we saw a soldier or a group of soldiers at some place, we did not know who they belonged to actually?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Some could be identified and others could not be identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just another question: Did you ever see Mario Cerkez in a black uniform?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No. I never saw him in a black uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that on one occasion in Sesvete in 1992 he wore a black jacket? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, did you ever hear of Mario Cerkez being a member of the HOS?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No, I never heard of that, and I know he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had he been a member, you would have known?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, I would have known for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm finished with that witness. I would just like to notice that there is an affidavit filed a couple of days before this testimony, related to this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Naumovski, have you any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I could finish by the time of the usual adjournment, not more than ten minutes. Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ceko, may I introduce myself once again. My name is Mitko Naumovski, I'm an attorney at law from Zagreb, and I defend Mr. Dario Kordic in these proceedings. I just have a few questions for you. Mr. Ceko, throughout this time period that you explained to us today, you were a soldier, essentially, all the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I wish to ask you the following, as an experienced soldier and officer: What was Mr. Dario Kordic, in your opinion; a soldier or a politician?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Mr. Dario Kordic, ever since I know him, was a politician, not a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Throughout your work in the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade and in the Viteska Brigade, and also during the time while you were in the Municipal Staff of the HVO in Vitez, did you personally ever hear of any commander, yourself included, having received an order from Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No. Throughout this period that you mention, from 1992 all the way up to the ceasefire, I never heard or saw, or saw and heard, that Mr. Dario Kordic issued some orders to soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us expand on this same question. Did any politician represent the civilian government either in Novi Travnik or in Vitez? So when we are talk being Vitez, I am talking about Mr. Anto Valenta, Pero Skopljak, Ivica Santic, et cetera? Did any of these civilians, politicians, issue any military orders to the brigade or could he have or could they have?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: All the persons you mentioned could not have issued military orders nor could they have issued military orders nor do I know of them having issuing military orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ceko, I assume that throughout this period of the war and before that, you probably had the opportunity of following the press conferences that Mr. Kordic took part in?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear at these press conferences or through statements on some other occasion that Mr. Kordic ever spoke in a derogatory insulting way about Muslims as a people?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No, I never heard of Mr. Kordic speaking in an insulting and provocative way about Muslims, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We also talked -- a few minutes ago, we talked about the civilian authorities and the military authorities, and you talked about that during your examination-in-chief so perhaps just one question. Specifically in Vitez, was there the civilian HVO and the military HVO or was this one body?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: The HVO was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, could you explain this to me a bit? In Vitez, was there a military authority and was there a civilian authority, and were they organised separately or not?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: There was a civilian authority and there was a military authority, and all of that was the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly there was the civilian authority we mentioned the persons --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel has overlapped the witness' answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are not supposed to overlap each other, you see. So there was a civilian authority and there was a military authority. And this military authority, you were also a member; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned this roadblock in Ahmici on the 19th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Mr. Dario Kordic in connection with this roadblock threatening the villagers of Ahmici that their village would be burned down if this roadblock was not removed?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put this same question to all the witnesses, perhaps it may seem strange to you, but I have to put it for reasons that we know. Throughout your soldiering, so to speak, in Novi Travnik, in Vitez as well, did you ever see any organised unit of the Croatian army in the territory of those two towns?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: No. I never saw any unit or any individual who was a member of the Croatian army either in Novi Travnik or in Vitez, nowhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ceko, you mentioned a few minutes ago going to the front line against the Bosnian Serb army, and you also talked about the defence of Jajce in this context.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to tire you with a long introduction and to tell you what the Prosecutor's case is, but my question is going to be very simple. The army of the Bosnian Serbs and the JNA, did they take Jajce through military supremacy or was this through some kind of bargaining between the Serbs and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Jajce was taken by the Serbs, the JNA. There was no agreement, no bargaining, no deal. We sent shifts up there and we realised that it was easier to defend ourselves further away from home than closer to our homes. And we would drive during the night without any lights and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, very well. So to put it simply, this was a military defeat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps yet another subject. In the territory of Novi Travnik and of Vitez, in particular, where you spent all of 1993 where you lived after all, can we agree that there were at least three major waves of refugees from the western or northwestern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes. Just a minute, what period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll get to that now. At the end of October, beginning of November 1992, there were many refugees coming in from Jajce, Kotor Vares et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the well-known events in Zenica and Travnik in 1993?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, then also in June, from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely that's what I wanted to ask you about. Tell me, please, just one more question. This major influx of refugees -- you are a man involved in logistics so you know about this -- these thousands of refugees, did they bring pressure on the resources that you had available in the municipality? Were there food shortages, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether this influx of refugees, notably in Vitez, led to an increase in the crime rate and crime as such?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Well, I did not think about this but for sure, yes, it was only logical that these were refugees who had lost everything and that they were involved in certain criminal deeds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems that in the transcript -- and this will be my last question. The last wave of refugees, you said when Travnik fell and surrounding villages and that was June 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ceko. Your Honours, I do not have any more questions, as I promised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we should give some information on the status of the witnesses, so should I do it on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do it on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I omitted one question, could I put it to the witness on Monday morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination on Monday morning. Mr. Ceko, we're going to adjourn now until Monday morning. Could you be back, please, at half past 9.00 on Monday morning to conclude your evidence. Would you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence, not to let anybody speak to you about it until it's over, and that does include the members of the Defence team. So if you would be back please at half past 9.00 please on Monday morning and I will remind the Court that we will be sitting two judges on Monday morning. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 1.03 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday the 31st day of July, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
